note: 392 studies mapped across eight harm domains, with a judgement on where AI is most likely to reduce harm.
title: The potential of artificial intelligence to improve patient safety: a scoping review

reading.body:
This scoping review maps 392 studies across eight harm domains and offers a judgment on where AI is most likely to actually reduce patient harm.

Mapping across eight distinct harm domains, rather than treating patient safety as one undifferentiated outcome, allows the review to identify that AI's safety benefit is uneven, stronger in some domains than others, which is a more actionable finding for a hospital deciding where to deploy AI first than a single aggregate safety score would be.

The review does not report which of the eight domains showed the strongest evidence in a way that substitutes for reading its own domain-by-domain breakdown, and as a 2021 review it predates the current generation of large language models used in clinical settings.

explain_beginner: The question, across all the different things that can hurt a patient in a hospital, infections caught during care, medication mistakes, blood clots, surgical complications, bed sores, falls, sudden decline, and missed diagnoses, how much has AI actually been tried, and does it show real promise. Researchers cared because they wanted a map of where AI effort was concentrated versus where the biggest safety gaps remained unaddressed, since AI development tends to follow what data is available rather than what harms patients most. The team screened 2,677 records down to 392 studies published through October 2019 and sorted them into eight harm categories, finding pockets of strong results, for example sensor based smell detectors combined with machine learning caught ventilator associated pneumonia with very high accuracy, and image analysis tools flagged risky surgical steps in real time. What it does not settle is whether these tools actually reduce harm once used routinely on real wards, since most of the underlying studies were retrospective and tested only on the data used to build them, not on new hospitals or new patients.
explain_business: Buyers evaluating AI patient safety tools now have a rough map of where evidence looks strongest. Adverse drug events, decompensation or early warning, and diagnostic error appear to be the domains with the clearest signal, since the review flags these as areas where existing prevention strategies fall short and AI has room to add value, while fall prediction tools looked weaker, with lab based accuracy of only 54 to 84 percent that has not been shown to translate into fewer real falls. The core risk to plan around, internal validation numbers reported in a vendor's own study can overstate real world performance by a wide margin, so a hospital piloting one of these tools should budget for its own local validation before trusting the marketed accuracy figure. Because so few of the underlying studies were prospective, procurement teams should treat this review as a starting point for asking vendors for prospective, externally validated evidence, not as proof any specific product already works. This is most relevant right now during vendor evaluation and contract negotiation, where the domain by domain breakdown is a reasonable way to gauge which vendor safety claims deserve the closest scrutiny before signing.
explain_practitioner: Method, a PRISMA style scoping review across multiple databases, 2,677 records screened down to 392 included studies, sorted into eight predefined harm domains including healthcare associated infection, adverse drug events, venous thromboembolism, surgical complications, pressure ulcers, falls, patient decompensation, and diagnostic error. Specific results include, within adverse drug events, deep learning models predicting reactions around 0.85 AUC and a neural network reaching 83 percent accuracy on warfarin dosing, within venous thromboembolism one algorithm hitting 89 percent sensitivity in cancer patients versus 11 percent for the standard clinical risk score, and within decompensation, gene expression biomarkers detecting sepsis at 0.86 to 0.92 AUC. In several domains the machine learning approach clearly beat the conventional tool it was compared against, including pressure ulcer prediction using random forests at 0.79 AUC against 0.68 for standard nursing assessment tools. The authors state plainly that most of these algorithms had not been externally validated or tested prospectively, and where external validation was attempted, performance often dropped, with one model falling from 0.90 AUC internally to 0.71 on an outside dataset, leading the authors to describe the overall evidence base as modest.
